item.title: Security policy
item.description:
Reporting a vulnerability

Do not open a public issue or pull request for a security vulnerability.

Email security@circleci.com, whether the problem is in Smarter Workflows or in the CircleCI platform. CircleCI’s security team receives the report. The project sets no response target, and CircleCI has no bounty program (process).

For a sensitive report, encrypt the message with the key at https://circleci.com/.well-known/pgp-key.txt.

Include the steps to reproduce, the release or commit, and the planner version (circleci-smarter version).

Supported versions

Smarter Workflows is at version 0.x. Fixes land on main and ship in the next release. The code and the design have not been independently reviewed or penetration-tested.

Support

Smarter Workflows is a CircleCI Labs project. CircleCI support does not cover it, and field engineers handle bugs and feature requests on a best-effort basis, with no SLA. Use GitHub issues for problems that are not security vulnerabilities.

What the planner does with your credentials and your repository

Limitations lists the known gaps in detail.

  • The continuation key (CIRCLE_CONTINUATION_KEY) is read only by circleci-smarter continue. It never prints the key or the request body, only the status code.
  • The impact map lists repo paths each job may read. It is built by circleci-smarter analyze, not by extra steps in customer jobs. Optional AI classification may send source contents to the provider; see the threat model.
  • The impact map lives in the project cache, and any branch can write a cache entry. A forged map could make the planner skip jobs. Mandatory jobs and the guardrails do not depend on the map, and every default branch run is a full run. Signing the map on the default branch is planned.
  • The guardrail bundle runs locally in the setup job, against the config that the planner generated. The same bundle can be enforced org-wide as a config policy.

item.title: 3. Build the impact map from file-access traces of full runs on the default branch
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-13. Status: Superseded by ADR 8.

Context

Smarter Testing builds an impact map on the default branch, then uses it on other branches to pick the tests a change affects. This project wants the same loop for jobs:

  1. a full run on the default branch rebuilds the map;
  2. branches use it;
  3. a merge triggers the next full run, which rebuilds it again.

A job’s equivalent of test coverage is the set of repo files it reads. There are several ways to record that:

  • Hand-written globs go stale.
  • Language analyzers need one per ecosystem, and miss scripts and config files.
  • strace and LD_PRELOAD are slow, and Go binaries bypass libc.
  • fanotify and eBPF need privileges that Docker jobs do not have.
  • Access times (atime) cost nothing. Under the usual relatime mount option, the first read after a write always updates a file’s atime. A freshly checked-out file has atime equal to mtime, so a file that was read has atime greater than mtime.

Decision

  1. On full runs of the default branch, the planner adds two steps to every job of the pruned workflow:
    • Right after checkout, a reset step sets the atime of every tracked file and directory to the epoch, because checkout itself reads every file. It also probes that atime works on that filesystem.
    • A post-step records the tracked files and the directories whose atime has since moved past the epoch: the ones the job read or listed. A job whose filesystem fails the probe gets an incomplete trace.
  2. A final job merges the traces into the impact map.
  3. It saves the map to the project cache under a key derived from the commit SHA.
  4. On other branches, the planner restores the map for the merge-base commit, falling back to the newest map.
  5. Only green full runs produce a map.

Consequences

  • No ML, no per-language code, no hand-written globs. The map explains itself: “this job read these files”.
  • noatime filesystems, busybox find and non-Linux executors give incomplete traces, so those jobs always run.
  • Because a read is “atime past the epoch”, an input that is read and then rewritten in the same job (a formatter run with -w) still counts as read. Traces still miss inputs from outside the repo: see ADR 2 for how those are covered.
  • Cache entries can expire (default retention) and can be written by any branch. A missing map means a full run. Mandatory jobs and guardrails do not depend on the map. Signing the map on the default branch is planned hardening.

Verification (2026-11-13)

Tested on CircleCI’s docker executor (cimg/base, overlay, relatime) and machine executor (ubuntu-2404, ext4, relatime):

  • After the checkout step, 43 of 44 tracked files already had atime newer than mtime, because checkout reads them.
  • After the reset step, a job that ran cat README.md; ls docs was traced as exactly README.md and docs.

item.title: Backtest
item.description:
The backtest command replays historical CI runs against today’s impact map and reports how often select mode would still have run failing jobs (recall) and how much job time it would have skipped (savings).

Method

For each record in a history file, the planner runs in select mode with the recorded base, commit, branch, and changed paths. That reuses internal/planner exactly as plan --mode select does; backtest does not duplicate selection logic.

For each job that ran in CI:

Outcome Meaning
Caught The job failed and select mode would still run it.
Miss The job failed and select mode would skip it.
Unmatched The job failed but its name is not in today’s workflow (renamed or removed); excluded from recall.
Flaky The job failed then passed on a rerun of the same commit; excluded from recall.

Recall is caught / (caught + misses) over non-flaky failures in jobs that still exist in the config.

Savings sums duration_s over matched jobs that ran historically but would be skipped, divided by matched recorded job time. Unmatched job time is reported separately.

History file format

A JSON array of commits:

[
 {
 "commit": "sha",
 "base": "merge-base sha",
 "branch": "feature/x",
 "changed": [{ "path": "pkg/foo.go", "status": "M" }],
 "jobs": [
 { "name": "go-test", "status": "failed", "duration_s": 120.5 }
 ]
 }
]

Optional per-commit parameters overrides the --parameters file for that pipeline (same semantics as plan --parameters).

Build a history file with circleci-smarter history fetch (or the fetch-history.sh wrapper). Set CIRCLE_TOKEN or CIRCLECI_TOKEN; optional CIRCLECI_HOST for server installs. The command pages pipelines newest first, resolves job outcomes (including flaky when a job failed then passed on a workflow rerun), and fills base / changed from a local --repo clone. Commits missing from the clone are skipped. Fixture parsing is tested by scripts/bench/test-parse.sh and go test ./internal/history/....

Diff base. For each pipeline commit C, base is the newest commit on origin/<default>’s first-parent chain (cached once) such that P ≠ C and P is an ancestor of C. A commit on that chain uses its first parent; if none applies, base is empty (no changed paths). Changed paths come from git diff --name-status -M -z (renames are a delete plus an add). This avoids empty diffs for feature-branch SHAs that were later merged with a merge commit—older histories that used plain merge-base had that bug.

circleci-smarter history fetch \
 --project-slug circleci/org/repo \
 --workflow ci \
 --limit 200 \
 --repo . \
 --out history.json

Command 

circleci-smarter backtest \
 --history history.json \
 --map impact-map.json.gz \
 --config .circleci/continue.yml \
 --workflow ci \
 --parameters pipeline-params.json \
 --mandatory security-scan \
 --format md

--parameters is a JSON object of pipeline parameter values, applied to every commit unless a history record carries its own parameters object. Use the same file you would pass to plan --parameters when the continuation config gates workflows or jobs on << pipeline.parameters.* >>.

--format json writes the machine-readable report (used for golden tests).

--strict makes backtest warnings fatal (exit 1). Warnings print on stderr and at the top of the report:

  • Workflow disabled: when --parameters turn off the workflow (when/unless false), recall is meaningless — every commit is treated as if the workflow did not run.
  • Job name drift: when more than half of recorded job outcomes do not match any job in today’s workflow (renamed jobs or wrong --workflow).

Scheduled benchmark on main

The benchmark workflow in .circleci/continue.yml runs when pipeline.trigger.type is schedule (the schedule is configured on the project in CircleCI, not in this file). It uses the smarter-workflows-ai context so fetch-history.sh can call the API with << pipeline.project.slug >> (GitHub App projects use the circleci/org/project form). It restores the latest impact map cache, fetches the last 200 ci pipelines, runs backtest, and stores backtest.md and backtest.json as artifacts.

Limits of replay

  • One map for all commits. The map reflects the repo layout at its revision (usually recent main). Older commits that touched different paths or job names are approximate.
  • Changed files only. History carries a file list, not full git trees. Adds/deletes may miss directory moves the live planner would see via git ls-tree.
  • Workflow drift. Failures in jobs removed from the config or renamed are unmatched (listed separately, not in recall). Savings count only jobs present in today’s workflow.
  • Parameter gates. Without --parameters, workflow when expressions that depend on pipeline parameters may be unknown, which forces a full run and makes savings look like 0%.
  • No guardrail replay. Backtest does not pass --policy-bundle; historical guardrail repairs are not simulated.
  • Flaky detection depends on CircleCI job rerun metadata when history is mined; hand-written fixtures set "flaky": true explicitly.

Use backtest to compare maps and tuning over time, not as a guarantee for every past commit.

Measured: this repository (2026-11-15)

Replayed 79 commits from the project’s ci workflow against the impact map from main at commit 83d7d6082:

Metric Value
Failures (non-flaky) 5
Caught 5
Misses 0
Flaky (excluded) 0
Recall 100%
Historical job time 13 737 s
Would have skipped 949 s
Savings 6.9%

History here is mostly Go and .circleci/ changes, which reach most jobs, so skipped time stays small. Replaying the demo monorepo history would not measure much: those pipelines already ran in select mode when the traces were taken.

item.title: Learn
item.description:
circleci-smarter learn is the scheduled job that refreshes the learned layer (AI mappings and history corrections) and estimates how select mode would behave on recent pipelines.

Command 

circleci-smarter learn --project-slug gh/org/repo --workflow ci --limit 50 \
 --repo . --config .circleci/continue.yml \
 --learned /tmp/smarter/learned.json --learned-out /tmp/smarter/learned-new.json \
 --report learn.md --report-json learn.json

Use --history FILE to skip the API and replay a saved history file (no token). --history-out stores what was fetched. --parameters FILE sets pipeline parameter values for every replayed commit.

AI modes match analyze (auto, on, off, dry-run). --min-recall exits with code 3 when projected recall is below the threshold.

Report

The Markdown and JSON reports open with what was measured: how many commits were replayed, recall and projected job-time savings, misses before and after this run’s corrections, corrections added, incomplete jobs (with reasons), and AI usage (calls, tokens, estimated cost).

Local trial

Before enabling select mode in CI, run learn against your project slug or a recorded history file. Fix incomplete jobs and review misses until recall and savings meet your bar. Costs are dominated by the optional AI classifier; history fetch uses the CircleCI API only.

Costs

  • History fetch: CircleCI API calls only; no job minutes on your project.
  • AI: Billed per Anthropic usage when --ai is not off; see the report’s token and cost lines (Haiku tier, same pricing note as analyze).

See also Analyze for the learned layer format and Backtest for how recall is computed.

item.title: 8. Impact maps from analysis, not traces
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-16. Status: accepted.

Context

Tracing needs a step injected into every job. It only works where file access times work and where the image has the tools. On a real 39-job project only 4 jobs produced complete traces: images without git, and runner or machine jobs, were never traced. Users will not edit their jobs before they know the tool is worth it. From v0.3 the impact map comes from circleci-smarter analyze: static analysis of the config and the repo, an optional AI classifier, and corrections mined from past runs. Tracing goes away completely, which also takes a lot of complexity with it. v0.x allows breaking changes; the trace flags simply disappear.

Decision

  1. The map comes from circleci-smarter analyze, from three sources:
    • static analysis of the config and the repo (run commands and the scripts they call, Go imports, Node and Python manifests, Dockerfile COPY, working_directory, orb parameters such as app-dir, cache-key checksum files, workspace data flow, path-filtering mappings);
    • an optional AI classifier, given the job definitions, the repo tree and the source contents, which returns inputs with a confidence;
    • corrections mined from past runs: a job that failed on a change its map could not see gains that change’s paths, unless the failure was flaky.
  2. The static part is computed fresh in the setup job. A learned layer (the AI inputs and the corrections) is refreshed by a weekly learn job.
  3. No existing job is edited.
  4. A job is skipped only when proven:
    • static analysis understood every step of the job: each command is a recognized tool, a benign builtin or a script it followed, and each input resolved to a path that exists at the revision. A step it does not understand (an unknown binary, make, an orb command outside the known table) makes the job unknown;
    • coverage that comes only from the AI needs a confidence of at least the threshold (0.8 by default), a job hash that matches the current job definition, and at least one valid input;
    • otherwise the job is unknown and runs.
  5. Shadow mode first, and a backtest on real history before select mode.

Consequences

  • onboarding needs no job edits, and works on every executor and image;
  • the map can be built and checked locally before anything changes in CI;
  • static analysis misses dynamic inputs (paths built from environment variables, network fetches): the AI layer, the history corrections and shadow mode cover that;
  • source contents go to the AI provider when the AI is on (see the threat model);
  • the trace flags are gone in v0.3.

item.title: How it works
item.description:
The loop 

weekly learn ──► history + analyze (AI + corrections) ──► learned layer artifact
│
push ──► setup: plan ──► analyze at HEAD (static + learned layer) ──► impact map in memory
│ │
├─ select + optional plan-time AI review (add-only)
├─ guardrails pre-flight (policies/), repair or full run
└─ continue: pruned workflow + smarter-gate

  1. Plan builds a fresh map. In each pipeline, circleci-smarter plan runs static analysis at HEAD through the analyze library (AI off), merging the cached learned layer when --learned is set. You can still pass --map to use a pre-built file. The plan report lists input counts and sources for skipped jobs.

  2. Learn refreshes the slow layer. On a schedule, circleci-smarter learn fetches recent workflow history, runs analyze with AI and history corrections, writes an updated learned layer, and backtests recall and savings. Its report is the trial run before you trust select mode.

  3. A branch gets a plan. The plan job:

    1. finds the merge-base with the default branch;
    2. builds or loads the impact map;
    3. compares the changed files with what each job lists as inputs;
    4. optionally asks the AI to add skipped jobs (never remove) when --ai-review is on or shadow.

  4. A job runs when the change touches one of its map inputs (exact files, recursive input dirs, or repository root .). Added, modified, deleted, and renamed paths use the same rule. Mandatory jobs always run. So do:

    • the ancestors (requires) of every job that runs;
    • jobs that consume a workspace produced by a job that runs;
    • jobs with no map entry or inputs that do not meet the skip proof (ADR 8): static analysis understood every step (each command is a recognized tool, a benign builtin or a script it followed, and each input resolved to an existing path at the revision; an unknown binary, make, or an orb command outside the known table makes the job unknown), and any AI-only coverage needs confidence ≥ the threshold, a matching job hash, and at least one valid input;
    • job groups: an entry that names a group under job-groups runs as one unit, since v0.1 does not look inside it.

    Some entries run no steps: an approval (type: approval, on the entry or in the job’s definition), a no-op job (type: no-op) and a release job (type: release). They have no inputs of their own, so the jobs around them decide. An approval or a no-op job stays when a job that runs requires it. A release job stays when a job it requires runs: it tracks that job’s release. A no-op job that nothing requires, such as an all-tests-passed that you use as your required status check, always stays: it waits only for the jobs that stay, or for smarter-gate when none of the jobs it waited for does, so it never passes before the selected jobs have.

    A job that your own filters keep off the branch, or whose required jobs they all keep off it, does not run there whatever the change is, even when it is mandatory. The plan leaves it out and says so in a warning. A requirement on a job that does not run is ignored, as in CircleCI, and the plan drops it.

  5. Guardrails. The planner checks the config it generated against the Rego bundle in policies/, using CircleCI’s own policy engine (circle-policy-agent).

    • If a mandatory job is missing, it adds the job and checks again.
    • Any other hard violation turns the plan into a full run.

  6. The gate. Every planned workflow ends with smarter-gate, which waits for every selected job. The workflow always runs, even when only the gate is left.

    • The gate is a no-op job (smarter-gate: {type: no-op}): no executor and no steps, so it costs no credits and starts no container. It is CircleCI’s gatekeeper pattern for one required status check. It succeeds when every job it requires succeeds.
    • CircleCI’s GitHub App reports one check per workflow (e.g. ci - <definition>): make that check required.
    • If you use per-job status checks, require smarter-gate. Either way, a PR never waits on a skipped job.

When it runs everything

  • the default branch, tags and scheduled pipelines;
  • a change under .circleci/ (or another --full-run-paths glob);
  • no impact map, or no merge-base;
  • any planner error;
  • a head commit that contains [smarter full].

Modes

Mode What runs Use it for
shadow everything; the plan is only reported onboarding: see what select mode would skip
select only the selected jobs + smarter-gate after shadow mode convinces you

Each plan job stores smarter-plan/plan.md and plan.json as artifacts: every job, run or skip, and the reason.

Results on this repository (2026-11-14)

From the first real impact map:

  • No job reads the docs.
  • orb-validate reads exactly the orb, its validation script and the two CI configs.
  • go-test reads 106 files.
Branch change Select mode runs Why
docs only 1 of 8 jobs (security-scan, mandatory) + gate nothing else reads docs/
one Go package (internal/report) 5 of 8 go-test, go-lint and build read it; e2e-plan consumes build’s workspace; security-scan is mandatory
.circleci/continue.yml all 8 the pipeline definition changed

The docs-only branch in select mode spent 46 s of job time, against 280 s for the full run, about 84% less compute.

The numbers are from before the pipeline gained the job docs-site-build, which builds the docs site and reads docs/. A docs-only change now runs that job too.

Tools for agents

Two commands let an agent (or a person) read a pipeline and check a layout of it, with no plan and no impact map needed:

  • circleci-smarter catalog --config .circleci/continue.yml --map impact-map.json.gz prints the jobs of a workflow as JSON: each one’s kind, executor, contexts, filters, requirements, workspace use and, with a map, how much of the repository it read.
  • circleci-smarter layout check --config composed.yml --catalog catalog.json --policy-bundle policies --mandatory security-scan --restricted-contexts deploy checks how the jobs of a workflow wait for each other, and reports each problem with a code and a hint on how to fix it: a requires that points nowhere, a cycle, a workspace attached before it is persisted, a restricted context with no approval before it, a missing mandatory job, a gate that is not a no-op job or does not wait for every job that runs, and an approval that a branch filter can leave out. It exits 3 when there are errors. A plan the planner writes has a no-op gate and no structural problem that its input did not have.

The spec has the formats.

item.title: 7. Impact map v2: shared path tables and compact indices
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-15. Status: accepted.

Context

Impact map v1 stores every repo path verbatim in each job’s files and dirs arrays. On large monorepos the JSON grows with the number of job×path pairs (roughly jobs × average reads), blows past the 16 MiB parse cap, and takes seconds to decode. A realistic shape is thousands of jobs each reading a large fraction of tens or hundreds of thousands of unique paths.

Decision

  1. On-disk format v2 (still JSON, gzip-compressed as impact-map.json.gz):
    • Sorted files and dirs tables: each repo path appears once.
    • Per job, file_idx and dir_idx are standard base64 blobs of sorted delta varints over table indices (first index absolute, later indices encode the gap from the previous one).
    • Metadata unchanged: revision, created_at, method, and per-job complete and nodes.
  2. Why delta varints instead of bitsets: Indices are dense when jobs read many files but sparse when they read few; delta varints are small in the common case, need no third-party format, and decode in one pass with strict bounds. Roaring or raw bitsets win when sets are extremely sparse across a huge table; this workload is usually “many indices per job out of a shared table”, where varints are simpler and fast enough.
  3. Writers (circleci-smarter analyze and map build) emit v2 gzip only. Readers accept v1 JSON (legacy cache) and v2 gzip; plan tries impact-map.json.gz then impact-map.json.
  4. Caps (oversize or malformed → full run): compressed file ≤ 64 MiB; decompressed JSON ≤ 256 MiB; when compressed size < 64 KiB, decompressed must be ≤ 32× compressed (zip-bomb guard); ≤ 4096 jobs; ≤ 200_000 file table entries; ≤ 50_000 dir table entries; ≤ 100_000 indices per job per table; job names ≤ 256 chars. v1 maps keep the former 16 MiB uncompressed cap.

Consequences

  • From v0.3, planner input dirs are recursive: a dir input covers the whole subtree (repository root . covers every path).
  • Monorepo-sized maps fit in cache and decode in sub-second time on developer hardware (see docs/benchmarks-perf.md).
  • Path tables must stay sorted and deduplicated; corrupt index blobs fail closed at parse time.
  • Cache artifacts change extension; operators with only v1 files still work until the next default-branch map build.

Verification (2026-11-15)

go test ./internal/impactmap -run TestBenchMapV2FitsTarget on this branch: synthetic 2000 jobs × 10k files each, v2 gzip under 20 MiB and decode under 0.5 s.

item.title: Limitations
item.description:
Where the planner cannot decide, the job runs.

Static analysis and dynamic inputs

Mapped paths are directory prefixes: internal/foo matches any file under it, and . means the repository root (every change). Paths built from environment variables, runtime downloads, or opaque shell are invisible unless the learned layer or history adds them. Make, unknown binaries, and orb commands outside the known table mark a job unknown (it always runs).

Opaque or unfamiliar jobs

Orb jobs, self-hosted images, and steps the analyzer cannot follow stay unknown until AI or history completes the map. Shadow mode shows what select would do before you trust it.

AI is optional

learn and analyze can run with --ai off. Without AI, coverage depends on static signals and history corrections only. Plan-time --ai-review adds jobs only; it never removes static proof.

Learned layer timing

plan merges the learned layer from cache on every pipeline. Until the first scheduled learn completes, maps are static only (more conservative). First pipelines after onboarding may run more jobs than after learn.

History corrections from infrastructure failures

Failures whose root cause is infrastructure (for example a missing CI token, not the commit under test) can still add history corrections during learn. Corrections only make jobs run more often; they never remove static proof. The learn report lists corrections per job. Use a new learned-key-prefix when you want an empty learned layer instead of merging forward from a bad history window.

Costs

  • learn: CircleCI API calls for history; optional Anthropic usage during classify (see the report’s token and cost lines).
  • plan: Inline analyze each run (no AI by default); optional --ai-review calls Anthropic when enabled.

Other v0.x limits (unchanged)

  • One workflow is planned; others pass through.
  • Matrix jobs and job groups always run as units.
  • The learned layer is stored in the project cache (tamper risk; see Threat model).
  • Workflow when/unless need known parameter values (--parameters, branch, tag, trigger type).

Planned improvements remain in the README and ADRs (signing cached layers, richer orb coverage).

item.title: 4. The catalog is native CircleCI config
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-13. Status: accepted.

Context

The first idea was a new catalog.yml with metadata on each job. That is one more format to learn and keep in sync. The jobs, commands, executors and orbs a team uses already live in its CircleCI config, or in orbs it shares.

Decision

  • Select mode (v0.1): the catalog is the project’s own full continuation config (.circleci/continue.yml). The planner prunes those workflows and keeps the order, approvals, filters and contexts the team wrote.
  • Planner settings (mode, mandatory jobs, full-run paths, extra inputs) are parameters of the orb job, not a new file.
  • Shared catalogs are orbs, pinned to exact versions: the only job-level units that cannot change underneath you.
    • URL orbs are allowed only when pinned to a commit SHA.
    • CircleCI functions are step-level units, so they are building blocks for compose mode, not jobs.
  • Compose mode (later): an agent wires jobs from a catalog orb (jobs, commands, executors) into workflows, and the guardrails bound what it can produce.

Consequences

  • Adoption means moving the pipeline into continue.yml and adding one setup job. No new schema.
  • What the planner generates reads like the team’s own config, minus the skipped jobs, plus the gate job.

item.title: Threat model (v0.3)
item.description:
Smarter Workflows runs inside a CircleCI project: setup jobs plan which jobs run on a branch, then continue the pipeline. This page is generic; it does not describe any one org’s policies.

Assets

  • Repository source — integrity and confidentiality as for any CI job.
  • Continuation config — defines jobs after setup; may reference contexts and images.
  • Continuation key — authorizes continuing the pipeline.
  • Learned layer — JSON in the project cache (AI inputs and history corrections merged at plan time).
  • Plan and analyze reports — job decisions, analyze completeness, optional AI review.
  • Policy bundle — Rego guardrails before continuation.

AI data flow (optional)

When AI is enabled (learn, analyze --ai auto|on, or plan --ai-review):

Sent Never sent
Job definitions (commands, images, working directories) Paths matching deny rules (.env*, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa*, .npmrc, .pypirc, .netrc, …)
Repo tree and trimmed file text within token budget Binaries and files over 256 KiB (listed in tree only)
Diffs for plan-time review (add-only) Content matching deny rules

Keys live in CircleCI contexts the operator attaches to learn or plan; they are not in the repo. The CLI never logs API keys.

Learned layer and schedules

Only the default-branch scheduled learn job writes the learned layer to cache. Feature branches restore the newest matching prefix but do not run learn in the recommended layout, so PR content cannot change what gets skipped on other branches.

Plan-time AI review can only add jobs; it cannot remove static proof.

Cache tampering

Threat: A branch restores an old or forged learned layer claiming jobs are complete when they are not.

Mitigations: Mandatory jobs always run. Jobs without static proof run. Malformed learned JSON is ignored (full run or warning). Restrict contexts (smarter-workflows-ai) so only trusted jobs fetch history or call AI.

Residual risk: Optional jobs could be skipped until recall checks fail; operators should read learn reports and use shadow mode first.

Trust boundaries

Actor Trust Reaches
Scheduled learn on default branch Semi-trusted Writes learned layer to cache
Feature branch / fork PR Untrusted for cache May restore any cache entry
Planner binary Trusted by operator Reads config, git, cache; writes continuation
Anthropic (optional) Third party Sees only data the operator enables
Policy bundle Trusted by operator Evaluated locally

Other threats (unchanged)

  • Injection via generated YAML: gate and key prefixes use safe identifier rules; customer catalog YAML is unchanged.
  • Continuation client: HTTPS, no redirect follow, key redaction in errors.
  • Policy bundle loading: walk stays under bundle root; symlinks skipped.

  • Analyze

item.title: 5. A Go binary that is also a circleci CLI extension
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-13. Status: accepted.

Context

The tool has to be easy to adopt in production if product teams like it. The circleci CLI dispatches circleci <name> to a binary named circleci-<name>; Smarter Testing’s testsuite is one such extension. CircleCI’s policy engine is a public Go library (circle-policy-agent), so a Go binary can evaluate policies exactly the way the service does.

Decision

Ship a single static Go binary, circleci-smarter, that can be called directly or as circleci smarter. It links circle-policy-agent for the pre-flight. The orb downloads a pinned, checksummed release. Until releases exist, it builds from source.

Consequences

  • One language and one binary, with no runtime dependencies in the planner job.
  • Impact maps are built by analyze in the setup job, not by steps injected into customer jobs (ADR 8).

item.title: 6. Every plan passes the guardrails before it continues: check, repair, or fall back
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-13. Status: accepted.

Context

CircleCI config policies also evaluate the continuation config. Server-side enforcement needs the Scale plan, and a continuation the server rejects fails the pipeline after the setup job has already spent its one continuation.

Decision

  1. The planner runs the project’s policy bundle locally, against the config it generated, using circle-policy-agent.
  2. Policies in the bundle tag violations the planner can fix with a machine-readable code, e.g. [smarter:require-job=security-scan]. The planner applies the fix and plans again, up to 3 times.
  3. A violation it cannot fix turns the plan into a full run, which is checked again.
  4. If even the full config fails, the setup job fails with the violations listed, without continuing.
  5. The same bundle can be pushed as org policy, limited to the projects that opt in, starting with soft-fail.

Consequences

  • Guardrails work on every plan, Scale or not. On Scale they are also enforced server-side.
  • Policies cannot read parameters as values, so the planner emits literal config and never adds parameters.
  • Compose mode will reuse the same loop, with an agent doing the repair.
